# Multi-event test inputs

Two families here, made differently and used for different things. Mixing them up
silently invalidates a comparison, so check which one you have before trusting a diff.

## Family A — repeated real event (throughput sweeps)

Every event is the same real 50-track event from `data_fp32/embed_input.txt`, repeated.
So all per-event means must come out identical, which makes them a cheap correctness
check as well as a throughput sweep.

    embed_input_100.txt     100 tracks =   2 events
    embed_input_500.txt     500 tracks =  10 events
    embed_input_5000.txt   5000 tracks = 100 events

No golden file. They are **not** prefixes of the Family B files -- do not compare a run
fed one of these against a golden built from the other.

## Family B — synthesised, with goldens (numerical verification)

Generated by `aieml_batch/make_golden.py`. The first 50 tracks are the real ones
verbatim; the rest are Gaussian, matched to the real per-column mean and std, drawn from
one seeded stream (seed 1234). Columns 6..7 stay zero, as in the physics data.

    embed_input_1000.txt    1000 tracks =   20 events   golden_1000.{npz,txt}
    embed_input_10000.txt  10000 tracks =  200 events   golden_10000.{npz,txt}
    embed_input_50000.txt  50000 tracks = 1000 events   golden_50000.{npz,txt}

Because the random stream is sequential, **each file is a prefix of the larger ones**
(verified: max|diff| = 0). One stimulus, one reference; a smaller run compares against
the first N events of a bigger golden.

Regenerate with:

    cd aieml_batch && ./make_golden.py --tracks 50000 --out ../testdata

Keep the track count a **multiple of 50**. `track_accum` counts *slots*, not real tracks,
so a short final event averages padding activations in with its real ones and comes out
wrong by design (measured 8.0e-02 for a 20-track event). The script warns.

## The two goldens are different models

`golden_*.npz` / `.txt` model the **streaming** roll -- track 0 pairs with whatever
preceded it, carry chaining across events, plus the leading flush event. That is what the
hardware physically does, so this is what the board's own check must match to ~1e-6.

The notebook (`aieml_batch/notebooks/rtda_reference.ipynb`) builds a *second* reference
from the ONNX model, which rolls **circularly** inside each event. That is the physics
truth. The two disagree on the first 3 tracks of every event by construction; the notebook
quantifies exactly that.

    golden_<N>.npz   means (n_events,128), y27 (n_events,27) -- for analysis
    golden_<N>.txt   "n_events 128" header then one row per event -- for RTDA_GOLDEN=

## On the board

`testdata/` is copied onto the SD image by the top-level `sd_stage` target, landing at
`sd_batch/testdata/`. `RTDA_INPUT` avoids having to overwrite `embed_input.txt`, which
matters because the SD partition is often mounted read-only and a failed `cp` is silent.

    RTDA_INPUT=sd_batch/testdata/embed_input_50000.txt \
    RTDA_GOLDEN=sd_batch/testdata/golden_50000.txt \
    RTDA_DUMP_EVENTS=1 ./host_batch.exe

`RTDA_GOLDEN` verifies on-board and prints a pass/fail, so you do not have to copy 1000
result files off the card just to diff them. `RTDA_DUMP_EVENTS=1` writes them anyway if
you want them locally.

Watch the `launch/DMA overhead` line in the report: ~583 us is paid once per
`graph.run()`, so it dominates a single 50-track event (95%) and fades to 11% at 10,000
tracks. That fixed cost is host-side and says nothing about the array.
